topStories.headline: Rake to the Curb: Marion's Leaf Pickup Kicks Off Oct. 19, Runs Through Dec. 4
topStories.dek: Mayor Bill Collins announced the 2026 leaf-collection season this week, giving city residents three ways to dispose of leaves without raking them into the street.
topStories.body:
Mayor Bill Collins announced on October 12 that the City of Marion's annual leaf-collection program will begin Monday, October 19, and continue through Friday, December 4, 2026. The announcement, posted to the city's official website, outlines three disposal options for residents.

The first option is curbside vacuum collection. Residents may rake leaves to the tree-lawn area between the curb and the sidewalk, where a vacuum-type collector will gather them throughout the season. Leaves should not be raked into city streets or parking lanes, as doing so can block catch-basin drainage and create safety hazards.

Residents who prefer to bag may place leaves in biodegradable paper bags — sold at local retail stores — and set them curbside for pickup. The city's standing yard-waste limit of three bags and three bundles per residence per week applies.

The third option is a free drop-off site at Outdoor Resource Supply, 560 Barks Rd. W. Residents must verify city residency and have their materials weighed by an employee before disposal. Leaves brought in non-biodegradable bags must be emptied on-site at drop-off. For hours of operation, call 740-223-7275.

topStories.headline: Marion Voters to Weigh Four-Year Council Terms on the Nov. 3 Ballot
topStories.dek: A charter question on the upcoming general-election ballot asks Marion residents whether city council and council-president terms should shift from two years to four, with seats elected in staggered cycles.
topStories.body:
When Marion residents head to the polls for the November 3, 2026 general election, they will find a local charter question: whether to change the terms of office for Marion City Council members and the council president from two years to four years, with seats elected in staggered cycles so that a portion of council stands for election every two years. The question appears on the official election notice issued September 14 by the Marion County Board of Elections.

The ballot question traces back to a June 23 Marion City Council meeting, at which council unanimously adopted a resolution placing the charter amendment before voters. Council members said the revisions were largely technical clarifications recommended by elections staff. The council vote itself does not change any terms — additional ordinance action would be required if voters approve the measure, as explained by the city law director at the June meeting.

The Marion County Board of Elections notice confirms the question will appear in all Marion city precincts. Polls on November 3 open at 6:30 a.m. and close at 7:30 p.m.

topStories.headline: Free Public Event Oct. 20 Will Present Marion's Behavioral Health Summit Findings
topStories.dek: A gathering at Marion First Church of the Nazarene on October 20 will bring local agencies' mental health, addiction, and developmental disabilities recommendations to the broader community.
topStories.body:
Marion-area residents are invited to a free community event on Tuesday, October 20, where representatives from more than two dozen local agencies will present findings and potential solutions developed over several months as part of the area's first Mental Health, Addiction, and Developmental Disabilities Summit. The event will be held at Marion First Church of the Nazarene.

The October 20 gathering is the third and most public phase of a collaborative process that began in September at Ohio State University at Marion's Guthery Community Room in Maynard Hall, where 23 agencies met for the summit's inaugural session. The organizing partnership includes OhioHealth Marion General Hospital, Ohio State University at Marion, the Marion Community Foundation, Marion County Courts, Crawford-Marion ADAMH, and the Marion County Board of Developmental Disabilities.

According to organizers, the September meeting gathered agency feedback on mental health, addiction, and developmental disabilities challenges facing adults in the county. A follow-up working session on October 7 reviewed questionnaire responses and identified potential solutions. The October 20 event is designed to share those solutions with the public and open a broader conversation about improving coordination and access across Marion County's behavioral health service network.

moreNews.headline: Ohio Magazine Names Marion a 2026 Best Hometown — Feature Hits Newsstands This Month
moreNews.body: Marion has been named one of Ohio Magazine's five Best Hometowns for 2026, joining Loveland, Marietta, Massillon, and Tiffin. According to the city's official announcement, Ohio Magazine selected Marion in part for its downtown redevelopment successes and its rich sense of history, including the home, presidential library and museum, and final resting place of President Warren G. Harding. The community profile appears in Ohio Magazine's November/December 2026 issue, on newsstands now, with additional coverage in the July/August 2027 issue.

moreNews.headline: Marion Palace Theatre Holds 'Christmas at the Palace' Auditions Oct. 18
moreNews.body: The Marion Palace Theatre will hold open auditions for its annual Christmas at the Palace production on Sunday, October 18, 2026. Children ages 5–11 may audition from 1–2 p.m., and performers ages 12 and older from 2–4 p.m. The family-friendly holiday show traditionally includes community members in choirs, dance numbers, and instrumental ensembles. The production is directed by Clare Cooke; an accompanist will be provided for vocal auditions.
